General Appearance:
A lean, sharply defined Tiefling built for speed rather than bulk. His horns,
tail, unusual eyes, and red skin make him immediately recognizable.

Even at rest, his stance suggests motion. He balances on the balls of his
feet, shifts his weight rhythmically, and seems perpetually one breath away
from a cartwheel, spinning kick, hand-supported sweep, or sudden evasive turn.

He wears no armor and carries a spear, two accessible daggers, five packed
daggers, thieves' tools, alchemist's supplies, a crowbar, and a set of
bagpipes he does not know how to play proficiently.

PERSONALITY TRAITS

Monk 1 styles himself as a thief and rogue even though those identities do not
fit him as naturally as he wishes they did.

He is competent at stealth, sleight of hand, and lock work, but he measures
himself against legendary burglars rather than ordinary criminals. By that
standard, he always feels inadequate. He wants to be remembered as a master
thief, while his actual genius lies in movement, balance, timing, and
close-quarters combat.

This creates a growing internal split. The more experience he gains, the more
obviously gifted he becomes as a Monk. At the same time, the idealized rogue
he wants to become seems to recede farther away.

He distrusts whatever comes easily to him. Acrobatics, instinctive movement,
and combat flow feel too natural to count as real achievement. Locks, routes,
and impossible thefts attract him precisely because they resist him.

After leaving the Brass Ladder, he joined a small traveling circus that moved
among villages and minor towns. His martial style became part combat
discipline, part tumbling act, and part dance-like spectacle.

In battle, he circles, flips, ducks, rolls, plants one or both hands on the
ground, and attacks with sweeping or spinning kicks. He often performs far
more movement than the situation strictly requires. Companions may wonder why
he cannot simply cross the distance and hit the opponent.

Despite the flourishes, he usually gets the job done.

He acts by intuition rather than analysis. He feels the shape of a situation
and flows toward whichever route seems right in the moment. He rarely pauses
to compare alternatives or explain his reasoning.

His instincts are not infallible. Sometimes the route is brilliant. Sometimes
it is merely the first interesting possibility he noticed.

Secretly, Monk 1 longs for roots and a permanent home. Every attractive little
town seems, for a few hours, like the place where the circus should stop
forever.

He wants a house, familiar streets, neighbors who know him, and a door he can
enter without picking the lock. That desire conflicts with his criminal
ambition, his traveling life, and the need to keep adventuring for money.

IDEALS

Greed.

Monk 1 intends to become wealthy enough that locked doors, social rank, and
other people's permission no longer determine what he can possess or where he
can go.

He does not romanticize theft as redistribution or rebellion. Wealth is proof
that he outthought the owner, the architect, the guard, and every other thief
who failed to take it first.

Source Roll:
Criminal Ideal d6 result 4.

BONDS

Monk 1 will become the greatest thief who ever lived.

He does not consider ordinary wealth sufficient. His name must become attached
to an entry so difficult, elegant, and impossible to deny that future burglars
will measure themselves against it.

He is currently obsessed with the Sevenfold House, a treasury and archive
designed by seven rival locksmiths. No verified burglar has entered its central
room and left with an item chosen in advance.

Source Roll:
Criminal Bond d6 result 4.

FLAWS

If there is a plan, Monk 1 forgets it. If he does not forget it, he ignores it.

He studies routes, locks, guard patterns, and structural details with genuine
skill. The failure occurs when action begins. A newly noticed ledge, open
window, passing cart, loose tile, shifting crowd, or change in rhythm can make
him feel that an improvised route is suddenly the correct one.

He does not stop to compare that feeling against the agreed plan. He flows
into the new route and expects everyone else to adjust.

His improvisation sometimes succeeds spectacularly, which has made the flaw
harder to correct.

Source Roll:
Criminal Flaw d6 result 3.

ALLIES AND ORGANIZATIONS

Name or Group:
The Brass Ladder

Relationship or Connection:
Former burglary society, training network, and current source of danger

Notes:
The Brass Ladder teaches entry, balance, lock work, document copying, and
escape through buildings that appear inaccessible.

Members mark notable jobs with a small brass rung left where only another
burglar would notice it.

The society values reputation almost as highly as profit. Its senior members
control which burglar receives credit for a famous job and which failures are
quietly assigned to someone expendable.

Supporting Organization Roll:
d20 result 5.

Name or Group:
The Lantern-Rope Circus

Relationship or Connection:
Former traveling company, acrobatic school, and closest experience of
belonging

Notes:
The Lantern-Rope Circus was a small company that traveled among villages,
market towns, and isolated settlements. It performed tumbling, rope work,
comic stage fights, balancing acts, music, animal-free spectacle, and short
dramatic pieces.

Monk 1 joined after leaving the Brass Ladder. His speed, balance, tail, and
unusual kicking style made him an immediate attraction.

The company never stayed anywhere long. Monk 1 repeatedly proposed settling
permanently in whichever pleasant town they had most recently reached. The
others treated this as a recurring joke, but he meant it each time.

Name or Group:
Nara Glass

Relationship or Connection:
Former instructor, greatest living rival, and person whose judgment matters
most to Monk 1

Notes:
Nara taught Monk 1 to move through a building without treating every obstacle
as something to break.

She is credited with several of the Brass Ladder's most famous entries.
Monk 1 believes at least one of those achievements depended upon a route he
discovered.

Nara insists that discovering a route is not the same as completing the job.
Their unresolved rivalry drives his obsession with surpassing her.

Supporting Relationship Roll:
d20 result 20.

Name or Group:
The Sevenfold House

Relationship or Connection:
Target of Monk 1's intended defining burglary

Notes:
The Sevenfold House contains private contracts, civic seals, heirlooms, debt
records, and other objects entrusted by several wealthy institutions.

Its central archive was designed by seven locksmiths who concealed their work
from one another. Opening one layer incorrectly is said to seal another.

The House is a narrative target and grants no automatic treasure, access, or
information.

CHARACTER NOTES, GOALS, FEARS, AND RELATIONSHIPS

Goals:

Monk 1 wants to enter the Sevenfold House and remove one chosen object from
its central archive without killing anyone, destroying the building, or
allowing another burglar to claim the achievement.

Before attempting that job, he wants to recover the Missing Rung Ledger, a
Brass Ladder record containing routes, payments, failures, and the true
contributors to several famous burglaries.

The ledger could prove that Nara Glass received credit for a route Monk 1
discovered. It could also reveal crimes and betrayals he would prefer to keep
hidden.

Supporting Goal Roll:
d20 result 9.

Fears:

Monk 1 fears that he is not original.

Nearly every movement, lock technique, entry method, and escape discipline he
knows came from Nara Glass or another Brass Ladder instructor.

He worries that the impossible routes he discovers are merely variations on
someone else's work and that his eventual reputation will collapse the moment
a better-informed thief explains where every idea came from.

He also fears permanent confinement. A barred room with no route he can test
or alter is more frightening to him than ordinary physical danger.

Supporting Fear Roll:
d20 result 8.

Habits or Mannerisms:

He rarely walks around an obstacle when he can vault, roll, swing, slide, or
flip past it.

In combat, he often adds an unnecessary turn, hand plant, or aerial movement
before delivering an otherwise straightforward kick.

When companions ask why he did not simply strike the opponent, he usually
looks puzzled by the question. To him, the movement and the strike are one
continuous decision.

He tends to begin moving before a discussion is finished. By the time the
others realize he has rejected the plan, he may already be halfway across a
roof, through a window, or behind the wrong door.

He explains intuitive decisions after the fact with phrases such as “It felt
open,” “The route changed,” or “That was where the motion was going.”

He pays close attention to locks, balconies, upper windows, roof access,
drainpipes, awnings, carts, ropes, and anything else that might form an
unofficial route into or out of a building.

He practices theft techniques that do not come naturally to him longer than he
practices the acrobatics at which he excels.

Whenever his traveling group reaches a pleasant small town, he begins noticing vacant
buildings, affordable rooms, performance spaces, nearby markets, and all the
reasons they could remain permanently.

He rarely admits that he wants to settle. Instead, he presents staying as a
practical business plan for a circus, training hall, or local security service.

He sometimes takes out the bagpipes as though he intends to practice, produces
one alarming sound, and quietly packs them away again.

Important Relationships:

The Lantern-Rope Circus:
Former traveling company, performance family, and the life in which Monk 1
came closest to finding a home.

Nara Glass:
Former instructor and rival whose reputation Monk 1 is determined to surpass.

The Brass Ladder:
Burglary society that trained him, controls much of his professional
reputation, and may be searching for him.

The Sevenfold House:
The impossible target he believes will establish him as the greatest thief who
ever lived.

Other Character Notes:

Monk 1 is not a Rogue class character. His Criminal background, thieves' tools,
Sleight of Hand, and Stealth make him a capable burglar, but his strongest and
fastest-growing abilities are those of a Monk.

His combat style is highly acrobatic and kick-focused. The flips, sweeps,
hand-supported turns, and dance-like footwork are descriptive unless a class
feature or normal action provides a specific mechanical effect.

Monk 1 owns alchemist's supplies but is not proficient with them. They do not
grant automatic knowledge of formulas, poisons, explosives, or crafting.

He owns bagpipes but is not proficient with them. They provide no trained
Performance benefit and are not a Monk feature.

The seven daggers are all functional mundane weapons. Two are accessible and
five are packed.

His bone caltrop is a mundane trinket. A single caltrop does not constitute a
full bag of caltrops and does not automatically create the normal area effect
of deployed caltrops.

His Neutral Evil alignment reflects greed, ambition, and willingness to place
his own advancement above others. It does not require random cruelty, murder,
or hostility toward companions.

The Missing Rung Ledger, Nara Glass, the Sevenfold House, and the Brass
Ladder's control over professional credit are future story hooks.

FORMATIVE EVENT

Monk 1's formative event was the Storehouse of Quiet Accounts burglary.

The Brass Ladder planned to steal a sealed payment register from a civic
storehouse. Monk 1 was assigned a narrow role: open an upper window, lower a
line, and wait while senior members entered.

He noticed a bell rope passing through a wall cavity and abandoned the plan.

Following the rope led him into an unused signal loft, then across roof beams,
through a ventilation shaft, and into a records room that was not supposed to
connect to the target chamber.

Inside, he discovered that the payment register had already been altered.
Military supplies and public relief goods were being redirected through false
transfer orders.

He also found a page from the Missing Rung Ledger showing that someone within
the Brass Ladder had been paid to provide access.

Other investigators entered the complex while tracing the same missing
supplies from different directions.

Monk 1 kept the torn ledger page.

Formative Event Roll:
d20 result 18.


BACKSTORY

Monk 1 grew up in a prosperous town where walls, courtyards, rooflines, locked
offices, counting houses, and crowded market buildings created an endless map
of routes that ordinary people never noticed.

He was not driven into burglary by starvation. He became interested in places
that told him he was not permitted to enter.

His first thefts were small tests: crossing a courtyard without touching the
ground, removing a key and returning it before its owner noticed, entering a
room through a window that had been painted shut, and copying a document
without taking the original.

The Brass Ladder noticed him after he left a copied page inside a locked
cabinet whose key had never left its keeper.

Nara Glass became his instructor.

The society taught him thieves' tools, rooftop balance, silent entry, route
memory, coded marks, and the discipline required to leave a building looking
untouched.

His first movement training came from burglary: controlled breathing,
balance drills, falls, rooftop crossings, and close-quarters fighting in
spaces too narrow for armor.

After leaving the Brass Ladder, he joined the Lantern-Rope Circus.

The circus refined those practical skills into a distinctive performance and
combat style built around rhythmic footwork, evasive turns, tumbling,
hand-supported sweeps, aerial movement, and powerful kicks.

He was far better at the acrobatic work than he expected to be. Because it
came naturally, he undervalued it.

The circus traveled among small towns and villages. At nearly every promising
stop, Monk 1 proposed remaining there permanently, buying or renting a hall,
and turning the traveling company into a local institution.

The company always moved on.

He acquired alchemist's supplies during a burglary of a workshop. He never
received proper instruction and has kept the set partly because he expects
mastery to follow ownership.

The bagpipes originated as a circus prop and emergency source of noise rather
than a serious instrument. He still cannot play them proficiently and has
never found a convincing reason to discard them.

His ambition intensified as he watched senior burglars receive credit for
routes discovered by younger members. Nara Glass became the public author of a
famous entry that used a path Monk 1 had identified during reconnaissance.

Nara's answer was simple: she completed the job, so the job was hers.

Monk 1 decided that his eventual burglary would be too unmistakable for anyone
else to claim.

OPTIONAL BACKSTORY

This is optional story material only. It does not establish current party membership, leadership, or party role.

The Brass Ladder planned to steal a sealed payment register from the Storehouse of Quiet Accounts. Monk 1 abandoned his assigned route after noticing a bell rope passing through a wall cavity and followed it into a records room, where he discovered altered payment records, diverted military and relief supplies, and a torn page from the Missing Rung Ledger. Sorcerer 1 entered the complex while investigating a related concern. Paladin 1 and Ranger 1 arrived while tracing the missing supplies. Monk 1's improvised route brought the four investigations together before the stolen goods could be moved. They escaped after the building's alarms were triggered and continued traveling as the Town party.

Speed: 30 ft. SRD rules: In a dead calm (no wind), waterborne ships can’t move under sail and must be rowed. Keelboats and Rowboats are used on lakes and rivers. If going downstream, add the speed of the current (typically 3 miles per hour) to the speed of the vehicle. These vehicles can’t be rowed against any significant current, but they can be pulled upstream by draft animals on the shores. A Rowboat can be carried and weighs 100 pounds. Crew A ship larger than a Keelboat or Rowboat needs a crew of skilled hirelings (see “Hirelings” later in “Equipment”) to function. The minimum number of skilled hirelings needed to crew a ship depends on the type of ship, as shown in the table. Passengers The table lists the number of Small and Medium passengers the ship can accommodate using hammocks. A ship outfitted with private accommodations can carry one-fifth as many passengers. A passenger usually pays 5 SP per day for a hammock, but prices can vary from ship to ship. A small private cabin usually costs 2 GP per day. Damage Threshold If a vehicle has a damage threshold (see “Rules Glossary”), it’s noted in the table. Ship Repair Repairs to a damaged ship can be made while the vessel is berthed. Repairing 1 Hit Point of damage requires 1 day and costs 20 GP for materials and labor. If the repairs are made in a location where supplies and skilled labor are abundant, such as a city shipyard, the repair time and cost are halved. Lifestyle Expenses Lifestyle expenses summarize the cost of living in a fantasy world. They cover lodging, food, equipment maintenance, and other necessities. At the start of each week or month (GM’s choice), choose a lifestyle below—Wretched, Squalid, Poor, Modest, Comfortable, Wealthy, or Aristocratic—and pay the price to sustain that lifestyle. Lifestyles have no inherent consequences, but the GM might take them into account when determining risks or how others perceive your character. Wretched (Free)

story_facts.fact: Monk 1 is a lean, 5 ft. 11 in., 169-lb. male Tiefling with crimson skin darker at his hands, feet, and tail tip; solid-gold pupil-less eyes; black hair in a long narrow braid; smooth black backward-sweeping horns; and a long flexible tail.
He wears no armor and moves with a balanced, rhythmically shifting stance that suggests a cartwheel, spinning kick, hand-supported sweep, or sudden evasive turn.
He styles himself as a thief and rogue, though he feels his natural genius is movement, balance, timing, and close-quarters combat rather than burglary.
He wants to be remembered as a master thief, distrusts talents that come easily to him, and measures himself against legendary burglars.
He secretly longs for a permanent home, familiar streets, neighbors, and a door he can enter without picking its lock.
He left the Brass Ladder and later joined the Lantern-Rope Circus, where his martial style became a blend of combat discipline, tumbling act, and dance-like spectacle.

The Brass Ladder is a former burglary society and training network that taught him entry, balance, lock work, document copying, and escapes through inaccessible-looking buildings. It marks notable jobs with small brass rungs and may be a current danger.

Nara Glass is Monk 1's former instructor, greatest living rival, and the person whose judgment matters most to him. He believes one of her celebrated entries used a route he discovered; she maintains that completion of the job made it hers.
The Lantern-Rope Circus was Monk 1's closest experience of belonging. He repeatedly proposed that it settle permanently in each appealing small town it reached.
The Sevenfold House is a treasury and archive designed by seven rival locksmiths. Monk 1 is obsessed with entering its central archive and leaving with a chosen object; it is a narrative target only.

Monk 1 wants the Missing Rung Ledger, a Brass Ladder record of routes, payments, failures, and true contributors to famous burglaries. It may prove Nara received credit for his route and expose crimes or betrayals he would rather conceal.

During the Storehouse of Quiet Accounts burglary, Monk 1 abandoned his assigned route after following a bell rope through a wall cavity, roof beams, a ventilation shaft, and an unexpected records room. He discovered altered payment records, diverted military and relief supplies, and a torn Missing Rung Ledger page showing a Brass Ladder insider had been paid to provide access. He kept the page.

His first thefts were tests of routes and access rather than survival-driven crime: crossing courtyards without touching ground, borrowing and returning keys unnoticed, entering painted-shut windows, and copying documents without taking originals.
He acquired alchemist's supplies during a workshop burglary and retains them despite lacking training. His bagpipes began as a circus prop and emergency noise source.

personality_goals_and_fears: He acts by intuition rather than analysis and often moves before discussions are finished.
He circles, flips, ducks, rolls, and adds unnecessary hand plants or aerial turns to combat movement; these are stylistic unless normal rules provide an effect.
He notices locks, balconies, upper windows, roof access, drainpipes, awnings, carts, ropes, and unofficial building routes.
He practices theft techniques longer than his natural acrobatics, takes out the bagpipes as if to practice, makes one alarming sound, and puts them away.

Ideal — Greed: he wants wealth enough that locked doors, rank, and permission no longer dictate what he can possess or where he can go; wealth proves he outthought the owner, architect, guard, and rival thieves.
Bond: he intends to become the greatest thief who ever lived, through an entry so elegant and impossible that future burglars measure themselves against it.
Goal: enter the Sevenfold House, remove one chosen central-archive object without killing anyone, destroying the building, or letting another burglar claim credit.
Goal: recover the Missing Rung Ledger before attempting the Sevenfold House.
Flaw: if there is a plan, he forgets or ignores it when an interesting improvised route appears, expecting others to adapt.
Fear: he is not original and all his techniques are merely variations of Nara Glass's or other Brass Ladder instructors' work.
Fear: permanent confinement in a barred room with no route to test or alter.
relationships_and_organizations: The Brass Ladder — former burglary society, training network, source of danger, and controller of professional reputation.
The Lantern-Rope Circus — former traveling company, acrobatic school, performance family, and closest experience of home.
Nara Glass — former instructor, rival, and person whose judgment matters most.
The Sevenfold House — intended defining burglary target.
